analysis.one_liner: Extends minimum wage, overtime, sick leave, rest breaks, and anti-discrimination protections to America's domestic workers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 136 cosponsors — enough to pass the House — but it was referred to six committees and none ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: About 2.2 million housekeepers, nannies, home care aides, and other domestic workers are largely left out of federal labor law. This bill would repeal the exclusion of live-in workers from overtime pay, require written work agreements, guarantee up to seven days of paid sick time a year, require meal and rest breaks, protect workers' privacy and communications, ban forced arbitration in their contracts, extend civil rights protections to domestic workers, and create a hotline, training grants, and a federal standards board for the industry. It never received a vote in any committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health and personal care aides, cooks, and chauffeurs — most of whom are women, disproportionately women of color and immigrants, and many working in private homes with no written contract and little access to legal remedies. Seniors and people with disabilities who rely on Medicaid-funded home care would also benefit from a higher federal match intended to stabilize that workforce.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the federal overtime exemption for live-in domestic employees, extending minimum wage and maximum hour protections to workers who live in their employer's home.

Employers of live-in workers would have to give written notice of termination and either 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance pay, and provide reasonable access to telephone and internet service.

Households employing a domestic worker 8 or more hours a week would have to provide a written agreement covering pay, hours, breaks, and termination policies, and the agreement could not contain mandatory arbitration or non-disclosure clauses.

Domestic workers would earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness, caring for family, or escaping domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Workers would get a 30-minute meal break after 5 hours and 10-minute rest breaks every 4 hours, could not be docked pay for breakages or cash shortages, and would gain protections against retaliation and immigration-related threats.

The bill extends Title VII civil rights protections against employment discrimination to domestic workers and creates a federal hotline, occupational safety training grants, and a Domestic Worker Wage and Standards Board.

The bill's findings cite research showing average domestic wages around $12 an hour, that 91 percent of surveyed workers who faced problems with working conditions did not complain for fear of losing their job, and that fewer than 9 percent work for employers paying into Social Security.

analysis.who_pays: Households and agencies that employ domestic workers — including live-in staff — would bear higher wage, severance, scheduling, and compliance costs, plus liability for violations. Federal taxpayers would fund the grants, the standards board, and a temporary increase in the Medicaid match for home care services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households and agencies employing domestic workers

drawbacks.text: Households that employ live-in workers would owe 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance at termination, a significant new obligation for families whose budget already covers room and board.
The written agreement, scheduling, notice, and record-keeping requirements would impose real compliance paperwork on ordinary families that hire a nanny or aide, not just agencies.
The federal government would take on new spending: grants for a hotline and training, an interagency task force, and a higher Medicaid match for home care services.
The bill exempts shared living arrangements, family members, and certain small-scale caregiving, leaving gaps in coverage that workers in those settings would still fall through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a workforce that federal labor law has largely skipped — workers with no contract, no overtime, and documented fear of retaliation — and the costs fall mainly on the higher-income households and agencies that employ them, plus federal spending. The main honest objection is the compliance burden on ordinary families hiring a babysitter-level or part-time aide, though the bill's 8-hour-week threshold and family exemptions narrow that; the arbitration and NDA bans also remove tools some employers consider standard. On balance the benefits to a vulnerable, largely female and immigrant workforce outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to six House committees, but no committee ever held a markup or vote, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act in the House on July 29, 2021.
It was referred to the Committees on Education and Labor, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means, and a day later to the Health Subcommittee.
No committee took up the bill, no markup or floor vote ever occurred, and it died with the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
All 136 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households and agencies that employ domestic workers kept the existing rules: live-in workers remained excluded from overtime, no written agreements are required, and workers still lack federal sick time, break, and anti-discrimination protections.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act and recruited 136 cosponsors.

for.name: 136 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a numerical majority of the House.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee (Chair Rep. Bobby Scott)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 29, 2021 and never held a markup or vote on it; the five other referred committees also took no action.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors for the bill, leaving it with no bipartisan path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 136 cosponsors was a House Democrat and no Republican signed on, so the bill never had a vote — or a coalition — that could move it through committee.

industries.industry: Home care and staffing agencies serving Medicaid and private clients
industries.note: The bill would regulate how these agencies pay and schedule domestic workers, but it also raises the federal Medicaid match for home care services and encourages fiscal intermediaries, steering federal money through the industry. Workers and the seniors and disabled people they care for stand to gain together if the workforce stabilizes.

Live-in employers would owe 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance at termination, overtime pay after the exemption is repealed, written agreements, and break and privacy rules. Their savings under the current no-overtime, no-severance status quo are the workers' lost pay.

industries.industry: On-demand domestic work platforms (cleaning and care apps)
industries.note: The bill bars employers from penalizing workers who communicate directly with customers instead of through the platform's app, and bans mandatory arbitration and NDAs in written agreements — rules aimed at how these platforms operate. Their interest in controlling worker-customer contact runs against the workers' independence.
